questions.q: What is the time complexity of pushing an element onto a stack?
options: O(1) because elements are placed directly at the top.
O(n) because existing elements must shift down in memory.
O(log n) because the top position requires binary search.
questions.fact: Push adds an element to the top of the stack in O(1).
why: Push increments the top index and writes the value in one step.
No shifting occurs because the stack grows at the top end only.
The top index is known directly, so no searching is needed.

questions.q: How does the peek operation on a stack behave?
options: It removes and returns the top element from stack.
It reads the top element without removing it in O(1).
It searches the entire stack to find the maximum value.
questions.fact: Peek reads the top element without removing it in O(1).
why: Removing the top element is the pop operation, not peek.
Peek inspects the current top element while keeping the stack unchanged.
Peek only inspects the top item, without searching through other elements.

questions.q: What condition occurs when attempting to pop from an empty stack?
options: A stack overflow condition occurs.
A segmentation fault in memory occurs.
A stack underflow condition occurs.
questions.fact: Popping an empty stack is an underflow; pushing onto a full fixed-size stack is an overflow.
why: Overflow occurs when pushing onto a full fixed-size stack.
Underflow is the logical condition, handled before raw segmentation errors.
Attempting to remove an item from an empty stack causes underflow.

questions.q: Which data structure manages function execution contexts and local variables during execution?
options: A call stack managing nested function frames.
A FIFO queue processing calls in arrival order.
A binary search tree indexing function symbols.
questions.fact: Function calls are managed with a call stack.
why: The LIFO call stack pushes calls and pops when functions return.
Queues are FIFO; functions return in reverse order of invocation.
Function calls follow nested stack discipline, not tree ordering.

questions.q: Where does an enqueue operation insert an element, and what is its complexity?
options: At the front of the queue in O(n) time.
At the rear of the queue in O(1) time.
At an arbitrary index in O(log n) time.
questions.fact: Enqueue adds an element at the rear in O(1).
why: Inserting at the front violates FIFO and shifting would take O(n).
Enqueue appends at the rear pointer directly in constant O(1) time.
Queues do not support inserting at arbitrary indices.

questions.q: From where does a dequeue operation remove an element in a queue?
options: From the rear of the queue in O(n) time.
From the middle of the queue in O(log n).
From the front of the queue in O(1) time.
questions.fact: Dequeue removes the element at the front in O(1).
why: Removing from the rear describes a stack pop, not queue dequeue.
Standard queues do not remove elements from middle positions.
Dequeue extracts the oldest element from the front in O(1) time.

questions.q: What distinct capability does a deque provide over standard stacks and queues?
options: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
It sorts all inserted elements in ascending order.
It stores elements in non-contiguous disk sectors only.
questions.fact: A deque allows insertion and deletion at both ends.
why: A double-ended queue permits push and pop at front and rear.
Deques maintain insertion sequence rather than automatically sorting items.
Deques are in-memory structures, not restricted to disk sectors.
